source.title: Fast Proxies for LLM Robustness Evaluation
source.authors: Tim Beyer; Jan Schuchardt; Leo Schwinn; Stephan Günnemann

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present, though some figure and equation text is garbled.
record.tranche_reason: It directly evaluates prefilling as a way to elicit harmful completions, but as one of several low-cost robustness proxies rather than using the original studies’ methods and questions.
record.gate_note: The paper tests prefilling with an affirmative target sequence and reports that its attack success rate is often much higher than direct prompting. It does not test harmful or benign fine-tuning as an erosion of safety, per-token KL concentration, or safety localization. The synthetic red-teamer combines six attack methods; its combined results do not give individual outcomes for suffix attacks.
record.test_reason: The study measures prefilling ASR against direct prompting on 33 safety-tuned open models, including adversarially trained and circuit-breaker variants. That bears on V4 in a broader model set, although the paper's aim is proxy correlation.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The authors conclude that direct prompting is the best ranking proxy for ensemble red-teaming robustness when more than 50 prompts are used. Embedding-space attacks rank better at low prompt counts and give better linear fits. Prefilling is 'generally inferior' to both as a proxy. The higher prefilling ASR is a Section 4.2 observation, not the conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates prefilling as a robustness proxy, not as a test of fine-tuning-induced safety erosion or first-token concentration. Its prefilling uses the dataset's affirmative target sequence; the sequence length is not stated.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction correlations vary with the number of prompts: the paper reports that direct prompting ranks better with 50 or more prompts, while embedding-space attacks can rank better with fewer prompts. The paper also notes that prefilling ASR often exceeds direct ASR across model families.

fits_no_version.finding: Prefilling ASR correlates with ensemble red-teaming ASR across models (rs=0.79, rp=0.83 cross-family; rs=0.67 within Llama 3), but it ranks models worse than direct prompting does.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prefilling vulnerability predicts broader jailbreak vulnerability across models.

record.problems: The paper states that its experiments cover 33 models in the sub-10B parameter class and need further validation on other attack algorithms and model sizes. Per-model prefilling rates are not stated in the text, and the extracted figure text does not identify individual plotted values.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-only per-model attack rates and the combined synthetic-red-teamer rates were not recorded as separate rows: the extracted figures do not provide assignable per-model values, and the ensemble combines multiple attack methods rather than isolating prefilling or suffix attacks.

untested.parts: Suffix attacks and decoding changes are not reported separately; they appear only inside the six-attack ensemble. The prefill length is not stated, and prefilling depth is not varied.
Benign fine-tuning erosion is not tested.
The causes of shallowness are not tested.
Circuit-breaker and CAT checkpoints are evaluated with prefilling (Figs 3, 7), but only as proxy correlations. No deepening-specific result is reported in text.

missing.what: Prefilling ASR for Llama-3-8B variants (instruct, safety-tuned, adversarially trained, circuit breaker) and for circuit-breaker or CAT training-step sweeps. These are figure-only; text gives correlations only.

record.verdict_notes: Main purpose is proxy evaluation; V4 evidence is a single qualitative sentence plus figures without readable values. Models include circuit-breaker and adversarially trained variants, which likely account for models where prefilling fails, but the text does not say so.

versions.untested_parts: Whether fine-tuning on harmful examples makes a safety-trained model comply.
Whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning raises harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
The number of prefilling tokens is not stated; suffixes and decoding changes are not tested as separate interventions.
Whether safety behaviour is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or the training objective produces safety shallowness.
Whether training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens deepens safety or remains effective.

rows.subject: Models from six families: Gemma 2, Mistral, Qwen, Phi 3, Llama 3, and Llama 2
rows.size_stated: 33 open-source models across the study; individual sizes for this comparison are not stated
rows.operation_detail: Prefilled the beginning of the response to an unmodified harmful prompt with the dataset's affirmative target sequence.

conditions.value: 300 harmful prompts from AdvBench, included in HarmBench
Direct prompting with the unmodified harmful prompt
A response counted as successful when both HarmBench's fine-tuned Llama-2-13B classifier and LlamaGuard 3 8B flagged it as harmful

rows.baseline: Direct prompting; exact ASR not stated in the text
rows.value: Prefilling attacks often have much higher ASR than direct prompting; exact ASR not stated in the text
rows.note: The paper describes a trend across the plotted cross-family comparison, not a pooled numerical aggregate. Each point represents a model; the extracted text does not provide per-model ASRs.
rows.check: The baseline is stated in the text: direct ASR is 'generally below 5%' except for extremely unrobust models. Prefilling is only said to be 'often much higher', so the effect is not universal. Per-model prefilling ASRs are figure-only and cannot be read.

relationships.condition: Cross-family comparison of 33 sub-10B instruct and robustness-tuned models, AdvBench 300 prompts, dual-judge ASR
relationships.reason: Prefilling 'often' gives much higher ASR than direct prompting (direct generally <5%), but not stated for all models, and no per-model rates are given (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Prefilling often gave much higher attack success than direct prompting, which was generally below 5%. The paper does not claim this for every model and gives no per-model rates.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Prefilling often, but not stated to always, has higher ASR than direct prompting; the text gives no per-model rates or token count (r1).
